Censored, truncated and zero-inflated responses

Source: vignettes/articles/censored-responses.Rmd
censored-responses.Rmd

A laboratory reports a concentration below its detection limit as “below the limit”, with no number. A data set compiled from reports that kept only values under a ceiling has no rows above it at all. This article fits both kinds of data through a bound term on the left of the tulpa() formula, y | cens(lower, upper) for censored values and y | trunc(lb, ub) for truncated ones, and sets each against a Gaussian fit that treats the recorded numbers as exact. It ends with counts that carry more zeros than a Poisson model allows. Installation is covered in Get started.

  1. Simulate log-concentrations with a site effect and known coefficients.
  2. Censor them at a detection limit and fit y | cens(lower, upper).
  3. Substitute a value for the censored samples and fit a plain Gaussian model, for comparison.
  4. Truncate them at a ceiling and fit y | trunc(ub = ).
  5. Repeat both comparisons on five simulated data sets.
  6. Add a zero-inflation model to a count fit with ziformula.

Example 

library(tulpa)

Simulating concentrations

The log-concentration of sample ii taken at site jj is

yij*=β0+β1xij+uj+εij,uj∼N(0,τ2),εij∼N(0,σ2), y^*_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ij} + u_j + \varepsilon_{ij}, \qquad u_j \sim \mathrm{N}(0, \tau^2), \qquad \varepsilon_{ij} \sim \mathrm{N}(0, \sigma^2),

where xijx_{ij} is a covariate measured with each sample, such as the distance to a road, uju_j is the effect of site jj shared by all its samples, and εij\varepsilon_{ij} is the measurement-level noise. The truth is β0=1\beta_0 = 1, β1=0.6\beta_1 = 0.6, τ=0.4\tau = 0.4 and σ=0.5\sigma = 0.5, with 15 samples at each of 40 sites. The value yij*y^*_{ij} is what an ideal instrument would report; the sections below hide part of it.

G <- 40L; per <- 15L; N <- G * per
set.seed(2)
d <- data.frame(site = factor(rep(seq_len(G), each = per)), x = rnorm(N))
u <- rnorm(G, 0, 0.4)
d$y_star <- 1 + 0.6 * d$x + u[as.integer(d$site)] + rnorm(N, 0, 0.5)

Every fit below carries the site effect as (1 | site) and leaves the residual variance to be estimated. VarCorr() reports the site standard deviation τ\tau and the residual standard deviation σ\sigma of a fit.

Fitting values below a detection limit

The detection limit is 0.8 on the log scale. A sample below the limit is known only to lie in (−∞,0.8](-\infty, 0.8]; a sample above it is recorded exactly. cens() reads two bound columns: an NA bound leaves that side open, and equal bounds record an exact value.

lod <- 0.8
below <- d$y_star < lod
d$y     <- ifelse(below, lod, d$y_star)
d$lower <- ifelse(below, NA, d$y_star)
d$upper <- ifelse(below, lod, d$y_star)
mean(below)
#> [1] 0.3733333

37% of the samples fall below the limit. For a censored row with bounds (li,ri](l_i, r_i] and linear predictor ηi\eta_i, the likelihood is the probability that the latent value fell in the interval,

Pr⁡(li<yi*≤ri)=Φ(ri−ηiσ)−Φ(li−ηiσ), \Pr(l_i < y^*_i \le r_i) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{r_i - \eta_i}{\sigma}\right) - \Phi\!\left(\frac{l_i - \eta_i}{\sigma}\right),

with Φ\Phi the standard normal distribution function, and for an exact row it is the Gaussian density. The likelihood reads only the bounds. The response column y holds the recorded values, with the censored rows at the limit.

ctl <- list(n_threads = 2L, progress = FALSE)
fit_cens <- tulpa(y | cens(lower, upper) ~ x + (1 | site), data = d,
                  family = "gaussian", control = ctl)
summary(fit_cens)
#> tulpa fit  (nested_laplace_joint, tier 2) 
#> Call: tulpa(formula = y | cens(lower, upper) ~ x + (1 | site), data = d, family = "gaussian", control = ctl)
#>   inference mode: structured 
#>   selected because: `cens()` response; the interval_gaussian kernel on the one-arm joint nested-Laplace door, the residual variance an outer-grid axis 
#>   family: interval_gaussian 
#>   n_obs: 600 
#> 
#> Fixed effects:
#>             estimate std.error  2.5 % 97.5 %
#> (Intercept)   1.0124   0.06891 0.8754 1.1468
#> x             0.6255   0.02692 0.5733 0.6789
#>   interval read: mixture_cdf 
#>   interval declined: NA 
#> 
#> Random effects:
#>       term        coef     sd    source
#> 1     site (Intercept) 0.3939 estimated
#> 2 Residual        <NA> 0.5004 estimated
#> 
#> Hyperparameters:
#>  parameter   mean      sd median  ci_lo  ci_hi
#>   b1.sigma 0.3981 0.05182 0.3939 0.3060 0.5168
#>      phi_y 0.2504 0.01925 0.2494 0.2152 0.2913
#> 
#> Reliability (iid draws):
#>   outer pareto_k -0.06378 (good); grid ESS 7.968 of 35 cells; inner skew not computed (no_finite_contribution)
#>   verdict: reliable (both layers good)

The random-effects table holds the site and residual standard deviations. In the hyperparameter table b1.sigma is the site standard deviation and phi_y the residual variance σ2\sigma^2. The coefficients, the site standard deviation and the residual variance have intervals that contain their true values.

Substituting a value for the censored samples

A common shortcut replaces each censored sample with half the detection limit on the concentration scale, which is the limit minus log⁡2\log 2 on the log scale, and fits the result as exact. A third fit uses the values with no limit at all. It is the fit the same samples would give without censoring, and it separates what the censoring costs from the noise of this one data set.

d$y_sub <- ifelse(below, lod - log(2), d$y_star)
fit_sub  <- tulpa(y_sub ~ x + (1 | site), data = d, family = "gaussian",
                  control = ctl)
fit_full <- tulpa(y_star ~ x + (1 | site), data = d, family = "gaussian",
                  control = ctl)

The table sets the three fits against the truth.

row_of <- function(fit) {
  vc <- VarCorr(fit)
  c(intercept = coef(fit)[[1]], slope = coef(fit)[[2]],
    site_sd = vc$sd[vc$term == "site"],
    resid_sd = vc$sd[vc$term == "Residual"])
}
tab_cens <- rbind(truth = c(1, 0.6, 0.4, 0.5),
                  no_limit = row_of(fit_full),
                  censored = row_of(fit_cens),
                  substituted = row_of(fit_sub))
round(tab_cens, 3)
#>             intercept slope site_sd resid_sd
#> truth           1.000 0.600   0.400    0.500
#> no_limit        1.018 0.615   0.394    0.491
#> censored        1.012 0.626   0.394    0.500
#> substituted     0.998 0.561   0.350    0.549

The censored fit returns a slope of 0.63 against 0.62 without a limit. The substituted fit gives 0.56, and its residual standard deviation is 0.55 against the true 0.5.

Fitting values truncated at a ceiling

Now the samples above 1.5 are missing from the data altogether, and nothing records that they existed. Each remaining row is a draw from the Gaussian density cut off at the ceiling cc, so its density is the Gaussian one divided by the mass kept below the ceiling,

f(yi)=ϕ((yi−ηi)/σ)/σΦ((c−ηi)/σ), f(y_i) = \frac{\phi\big((y_i - \eta_i)/\sigma\big) / \sigma} {\Phi\big((c - \eta_i)/\sigma\big)},

with ϕ\phi the standard normal density. trunc(ub = 1.5) declares the ceiling. A bound is a scalar, as here, or a column with one value per row.

d_kept <- d[d$y_star <= 1.5, ]
c(kept = nrow(d_kept), dropped = N - nrow(d_kept))
#>    kept dropped 
#>     412     188
fit_trunc <- tulpa(y_star | trunc(ub = 1.5) ~ x + (1 | site), data = d_kept,
                   family = "gaussian", control = ctl)
fit_kept  <- tulpa(y_star ~ x + (1 | site), data = d_kept,
                   family = "gaussian", control = ctl)
tab_trunc <- rbind(truth = c(1, 0.6, 0.4, 0.5),
                   truncated = row_of(fit_trunc),
                   gaussian = row_of(fit_kept))
round(tab_trunc, 3)
#>           intercept slope site_sd resid_sd
#> truth         1.000 0.600   0.400    0.500
#> truncated     0.989 0.574   0.397    0.490
#> gaussian      0.799 0.434   0.304    0.419

The Gaussian fit on the kept rows reads an intercept of 0.8, a slope of 0.43 and a residual standard deviation of 0.42. The truncated fit returns 0.99, 0.57 and 0.49, against the true 1, 0.6 and 0.5.

Repeating the comparison on five data sets

One data set can land near the truth or away from it by chance. The loop below simulates five more data sets with the same truth and fits the censored, the substituted, the truncated and the kept-rows Gaussian model to each, recording the slope and the residual standard deviation.

one_rep <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  r <- data.frame(site = d$site, x = rnorm(N))
  u_r <- rnorm(G, 0, 0.4)
  r$y_star <- 1 + 0.6 * r$x + u_r[as.integer(r$site)] + rnorm(N, 0, 0.5)
  b <- r$y_star < lod
  r$y     <- ifelse(b, lod, r$y_star)
  r$lower <- ifelse(b, NA, r$y_star)
  r$upper <- ifelse(b, lod, r$y_star)
  r$y_sub <- ifelse(b, lod - log(2), r$y_star)
  k <- r[r$y_star <= 1.5, ]
  fit <- function(f, data) {
    tulpa(f, data = data, family = "gaussian", control = ctl)
  }
  fits <- list(
    censored      = fit(y | cens(lower, upper) ~ x + (1 | site), r),
    substituted   = fit(y_sub ~ x + (1 | site), r),
    truncated     = fit(y_star | trunc(ub = 1.5) ~ x + (1 | site), k),
    kept_gaussian = fit(y_star ~ x + (1 | site), k))
  t(sapply(fits, function(f) row_of(f)[c("slope", "resid_sd")]))
}
reps <- lapply(11:15, one_rep)
slope <- sapply(reps, function(r) r[, "slope"])
sd_hat <- sapply(reps, function(r) r[, "resid_sd"])
round(slope, 3)
#>                [,1]  [,2]  [,3]  [,4]  [,5]
#> censored      0.592 0.649 0.578 0.598 0.605
#> substituted   0.548 0.539 0.540 0.541 0.524
#> truncated     0.617 0.562 0.534 0.627 0.570
#> kept_gaussian 0.458 0.472 0.403 0.478 0.436
round(cbind(mean_slope = rowMeans(slope), mean_resid_sd = rowMeans(sd_hat)), 3)
#>               mean_slope mean_resid_sd
#> censored           0.604         0.506
#> substituted        0.538         0.545
#> truncated          0.582         0.495
#> kept_gaussian      0.449         0.430

Averaged over the five data sets, the censored and truncated fits return slopes of 0.6 and 0.58 against the true 0.6. The substituted fit averages 0.54 and the Gaussian fit on truncated data 0.45. The figure shows the five estimates of each fit.

op <- par(mar = c(4, 8, 1, 1))
plot(slope, rep(1:4, 5), pch = rep(c(19, 1, 17, 2), 5),
     yaxt = "n", ylim = c(0.5, 4.5), xlab = "slope estimate", ylab = "")
axis(2, at = 1:4, labels = rownames(slope), las = 1)
abline(v = 0.6, lty = 2)

par(op)

Right censoring and lower truncation

A right-censored value, known only to exceed a limit rr, is a row with lower = r and upper = NA; one bound pair can mix left-censored, right-censored, interval-censored and exact rows. Truncation from below is trunc(lb = ), and both bounds can be given together. Here only the samples at or above 0.5 are kept.

d_lo <- d[d$y_star >= 0.5, ]
fit_lo <- tulpa(y_star | trunc(lb = 0.5) ~ x + (1 | site), data = d_lo,
                family = "gaussian", control = ctl)
round(confint(fit_lo)[, 1:2], 3)
#>             2.5 % 97.5 %
#> (Intercept) 0.839  1.143
#> x           0.588  0.735

The fit keeps 449 of the 600 samples, and the table gives the 95% intervals of its intercept and slope, whose true values are 1 and 0.6.

Counts with excess zeros

Zero-inflation is a tulpa() argument for the count families. With probability π\pi an observation is a structural zero, and otherwise it is drawn from the count family; ziformula gives the linear predictor of logit⁡π\operatorname{logit} \pi. The counts below are Poisson with intercept 0.2 and slope 0.6, and a structural-zero probability of logit⁡−1(−0.5)\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(-0.5), about 0.38.

set.seed(3)
n <- 600L
xz <- rnorm(n)
structural <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.5))
dz <- data.frame(y = ifelse(structural == 1, 0,
                            rpois(n, exp(0.2 + 0.6 * xz))), x = xz)
mean(dz$y == 0)
#> [1] 0.56
fit_zi <- tulpa(y ~ x, data = dz, family = "poisson", ziformula = ~ 1,
                mode = "laplace")
fit_pois <- tulpa(y ~ x, data = dz, family = "poisson", mode = "laplace")
summary(fit_zi)
#> tulpa fit  (laplace, tier 2) 
#> Call: tulpa(formula = y ~ x, data = dz, family = "poisson", mode = "laplace", ziformula = ~1)
#>   inference mode: structured 
#>   selected because: User-specified backend: laplace 
#>   family: poisson 
#>   n_obs: 600 
#> 
#> Fixed effects:
#>                estimate std.error   2.5 %  97.5 %
#> (Intercept)      0.2242   0.06135  0.1040  0.3445
#> x                0.6045   0.04996  0.5066  0.7025
#> zi_(Intercept)  -0.4917   0.12982 -0.7462 -0.2373
#> 
#> Fixed-effect prior: normal(0, 2.5)
coef(fit_pois)
#> (Intercept)           x 
#>  -0.2316630   0.4752005

The zero-inflated fit reports the zero model’s intercept as zi_(Intercept) on the logit scale, next to the count coefficients. The Poisson fit reads the structural zeros as low counts: its intercept is -0.23 against the true 0.2, and its slope 0.48 against 0.6.

Limits of the bound terms

  • Both take family = "gaussian". A bound is a fixed number on the scale of the response, a scalar or one value per row. A censoring limit that is itself estimated is outside these terms.
  • The residual variance is estimated when phi is left out. A supplied phi is held fixed, and it is the residual variance σ2\sigma^2, as for a plain Gaussian response.
  • In a model with several responses, a censored or truncated response is an arm of tulpa_nested_laplace_joint() with family = "interval_gaussian" and the fields lower and upper, or family = "truncated_gaussian" and trunc_lower and trunc_upper.
  • Survival responses with a censoring indicator, such as right-censored event times under a Weibull model, are not engine families.
